title: US product-market rivalry shapes investment, markups, and industry concentration
source_unit: Universe of US public companies, firm investment, cost of capital, markups, product-market rivalry, mergers, and industry concentration

observations.period: US public companies; paper issued September 2026; merger evidence since 1995

denominator.unit: universe of US public companies; exact firm-year count not disclosed in the NBER abstract

competition_and_investment.unit: product-market competition is a key driver of aggregate investment and capital allocation

cost_of_capital_response.unit: cost-of-capital shocks produce heterogeneous investment and markup responses and affect industry concentration

monopoly_rents.unit: monopoly rents account for a large and rising share of firms' value

merger_capital_formation.unit: mergers since 1995 are associated with a modest decline in aggregate capital formation of merging firms

merger_markup_response.unit: firm-level markup increases after mergers are highly heterogeneous

observations.method: Dynamic structural model of heterogeneous multi-product firms with hedonic demand and network product-market spillovers, taken to the universe of US public companies.
observations.uncertainty: The NBER abstract does not disclose the firm-year count, industry-level estimates, effect sizes, or the full identification and calibration details. The paper is a working paper; modeled and estimated firm responses do not directly establish consumer prices, worker outcomes, or realized welfare.
observations.subgroup: US public firms and industries with different product-market spillovers, cost-of-capital shocks, merger histories, and markup responses.
observations.counterinterpretation: Changes in concentration, investment, and markups may reflect selection into public markets, demand and technology shifts, industry composition, or merger targeting rather than cost-of-capital changes alone; high firm value or markup does not by itself prove consumer harm.

related_sources.claim: US financial conditions can weaken firm insurance and increase labor-income risk.
Worker heterogeneity explains much of the variation in labor-supply elasticities and firm wage markdowns.
US product-market creative destruction passes asymmetric risk into incumbent-worker earnings and jobs.

boundary: This record adds a US firm-investment-to-market-structure stage. It does not establish causal consumer-price effects, worker pay or control, household room, political response, or whether any particular merger increased or reduced welfare.
